docs.title: K8s Autoscaling Workshop
docs.text: Optimize a Kubernetes cluster with Dynatrace Smartscape, DQL and a Workflow: find the workloads whose resource requests do not match what they really use, compute better requests from the observed p95 usage, apply them and watch the gap between requested and used shrink.

docs.title: What you will be able to do
docs.text: By the end of this workshop you can find mis-sized Kubernetes workloads in Dynatrace and right-size their CPU and memory requests from real usage data.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: Platform engineers and SREs who run workloads on Kubernetes and know kubectl. No Dynatrace experience is needed; DQL is shown, not assumed.

docs.title: What is already running
docs.text:
When you press Start, your environment is built for you:

Component Where Purpose k3d cluster your environment a single-node Kubernetes cluster Dynatrace Operator + DynaKube namespace dynatrace ActiveGate with Kubernetes monitoring: feeds Smartscape and the container CPU and memory metrics OpenTelemetry Collector (DaemonSet) namespace otel-collector receives OTLP from the demo, reads pod logs (filelog), enriches with Kubernetes metadata, converts metrics to delta and exports everything to Dynatrace opentelemetry-demo-light namespace otel-demo frontend, cart, checkout, payment, product-catalog, postgres, valkey and a k6 load generator 
flowchart LR
  subgraph cluster["k3d cluster (your environment)"]
    demo["otel-demo<br/>frontend · cart · checkout · payment<br/>product-catalog · postgres · valkey · k6"]
    col["otel-collector<br/>DaemonSet: OTLP + filelog"]
    op["dynatrace<br/>Operator + ActiveGate"]
    demo -- OTLP --> col
  end
  col -- "traces · metrics · logs" --> dt[("Dynatrace")]
  op -- "Kubernetes API · container metrics" --> dt
  dt -- "Smartscape + DQL" --> wf["Workflow:<br/>Smart K8s Resource Optimizer"]
  wf -. "new requests" .-> you(["you: applyRecommendations"])
  you --> demo

docs.title: The loop you will run
docs.text:
1. Check the environment and see your telemetry arrive in Dynatrace.
  2. Find the mis-sized workloads with DQL on Smartscape.
  3. Run the Smart K8s Resource Optimizer workflow in the Workflows app.
  4. Apply its recommendations to your cluster.
  5. Watch the gap between requested and used resources shrink.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: This workshop is Henrik Rexed's K8s-autoscalingWorkshop, using his opentelemetry-demo-light, migrated to the Dynatrace enablement framework so it runs in the Enablement app. What changed is listed in the repository README.

docs.title: 1. Check the Environment
docs.text: Your environment already runs everything the upstream workshop's bootstrap built: a Kubernetes cluster, the Dynatrace Operator with a DynaKube, an OpenTelemetry Collector and opentelemetry-demo-light under constant load from k6. This step makes sure all of it is up before you start optimizing.

docs.title: The demo application
docs.text:
Look at the eight workloads of the demo, and at the resources each container requests:

kubectl get pods -n otel-demo
kubectl get deployments,statefulsets -n otel-demo \
  -o custom-columns='WORKLOAD:.metadata.name,CPU REQUEST:.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu,MEMORY REQUEST:.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.memory'

Every workload requests a little memory and no CPU at all. The scheduler places pods by their requests, so these numbers decide how many pods fit on a node — whatever the pods actually use. Keep this table in mind: in step 4 you replace these guesses with numbers measured by Dynatrace.

Each workload also carries the annotation resource-optimization.dynatrace.com/enabled: "true". That is the opt-in the optimizer looks for — workloads without it are never touched:

kubectl get deployment cart -n otel-demo -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}' ; echo

The check below proves the demo app post-create.sh deployed is running — every one of its eight workloads has a Running pod (and so the cluster under it is up):

docs.title: The OpenTelemetry Collector
docs.text:
The demo's services are instrumented with OpenTelemetry and send OTLP to a collector in namespace otel-collector. It runs as a DaemonSet — one collector per node — because besides OTLP it also reads every container's log files from the node it runs on (/var/log/pods, the filelog receiver). Look at its pipeline:

kubectl get ds -n otel-collector
kubectl get cm otel-collector-config -n otel-collector -o jsonpath='{.data.config\.yaml}' | grep -A3 'pipelines:' -m1 ; \
kubectl get cm otel-collector-config -n otel-collector -o jsonpath='{.data.config\.yaml}' | sed -n '/^    logs:/,/exporters/p'
  • k8sattributes adds the pod, workload and namespace — and the resource-optimization annotation — to every span, metric and log.
  • cumulativetodelta converts cumulative counters to the delta temporality Dynatrace ingests.
  • otlp_http exports to your Dynatrace tenant with an ingest token that never left the cluster's Secret.

This check proves the collector is running on every node:

docs.title: Dynatrace in the cluster
docs.text:
The Operator deployed a DynaKube in Kubernetes monitoring mode: an ActiveGate watches the Kubernetes API and reports the cluster, its workloads and every container's CPU and memory usage and requests to Dynatrace. Nothing is injected into the demo pods — they are observed through OpenTelemetry only.

kubectl get dynakube -n dynatrace
kubectl get pods -n dynatrace

This check proves the ActiveGate is up — without it, Smartscape and the container metrics the recommendations are computed from never reach your tenant:

docs.title: 2. See Your Telemetry in Dynatrace
docs.text:
Two independent paths bring your cluster into Dynatrace:

  • the OpenTelemetry Collector ships the demo's traces, metrics and logs, and
  • the Operator's ActiveGate reports the Kubernetes objects (Smartscape) and the container CPU and memory metrics the optimization is computed from.

Every learner of a workshop shares one tenant, so each query below keeps only your cluster: its name ends with your session id, {{DT_SESSION_ID}}.

docs.title: Traces from the demo
docs.text:
Open a Notebook in your tenant and run:

fetch spans, from:now()-15m
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}")
| filter k8s.namespace.name == "otel-demo"
| summarize spans = count(), by:{service.name}
| sort spans desc

Every service of the demo shows up, named {{DT_SESSION_ID}}-cart, {{DT_SESSION_ID}}-checkout and so on — the session id prefix keeps them apart from your classmates' services. This check proves the collector exported spans from your cluster:

docs.title: Pod logs through the filelog receiver
docs.text:
The collector also reads every container's log file on the node. Those logs carry the file they came from — the proof they were collected by filelog, not sent by an SDK:

fetch logs, from:now()-15m
| filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}")
| filter isNotNull(log.file.path)
| summarize lines = count(), by:{k8s.namespace.name}
| sort lines desc

This check proves pod logs from your cluster reached Grail through the collector:

docs.title: 3. Find the Mis-sized Workloads
docs.text: A request is a reservation: the scheduler sets that much CPU and memory aside for the pod whether it uses it or not. Requested too high, you pay for idle capacity; too low (or not at all), pods are packed onto nodes that cannot serve them under load. Dynatrace knows both sides — the requests from the Kubernetes API and the real usage from the container metrics — so the gap is one query away.

docs.title: Usage against requests, per container
docs.text:
Open a Notebook in your tenant and run:

timeseries {
    mem_used = max(dt.kubernetes.container.memory_working_set),
    mem_requested = sum(dt.kubernetes.container.requests_memory),
    cpu_used = max(dt.kubernetes.container.cpu_usage)
  },
  by:{k8s.workload.name},
  filter: endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") AND k8s.namespace.name == "otel-demo",
  from:now()-30m
| fieldsAdd mem_used_p95_MiB = arrayPercentile(mem_used, 95) / 1048576,
            mem_requested_MiB = arrayAvg(mem_requested) / 1048576,
            cpu_used_p95_millicores = arrayPercentile(cpu_used, 95)
| fieldsAdd memory_used_pct_of_request = mem_used_p95_MiB / mem_requested_MiB * 100
| fields k8s.workload.name, mem_used_p95_MiB, mem_requested_MiB, memory_used_pct_of_request, cpu_used_p95_millicores
| sort memory_used_pct_of_request desc

Read the result:

  • memory_used_pct_of_request above 100 — the container uses more than it reserved. The node is over-committed; under pressure, these pods are the first to be evicted.
  • Far below 100 — reserved and idle.
  • CPU has no request at all yet, so every millicore used is unreserved.

The workflow you run next uses the same metrics, over 7 days and through Smartscape: it walks from each container to its pod and its workload, keeps only workloads annotated resource-optimization.dynatrace.com/enabled: "true", and recommends p95 usage × 1.30 — usage plus 30 % headroom.

The upstream notebook

The original workshop ships a notebook, Smartscape Resource allocation, with these queries and charts. It is in this repository as dynatrace/smartscape-resource-allocation.notebook.json; to use it, download it and choose Upload in the Notebooks app. Its queries are not scoped to your cluster: in a shared tenant you see every learner's workloads.

This check proves Dynatrace has your containers' usage and memory requests — the inputs of every recommendation:

docs.title: 4. Run the Smart K8s Resource Optimizer Workflow
docs.text:
Dynatrace Workflows run DQL and code on a schedule or on demand. The Smart K8s Resource Optimizer turns the analysis of the last step into numbers: per container, the CPU and memory request to set.

Task What it does collect_underutilized_workloads DQL on Smartscape: container → pod → workload, keeps workloads annotated resource-optimization.dynatrace.com/enabled: "true", joins 7-day p95 usage and requests compute_recommendations JavaScript: new CPU (millicores) and memory (MiB) request per container, p95 usage × 1.30

Changed from the original workshop

Upstream, two more tasks patched the manifests in each attendee's GitHub fork and opened a pull request, and merging it rolled the change out. Here no fork and no GitHub token are needed: the workflow shows the recommendations in Dynatrace, and in the next step you apply the same recommendations to your cluster from the terminal.

docs.title: Upload the workflow
docs.text:
A copy scoped to your cluster was written when this step opened. Print it:

cat .devcontainer/yaml/gen/smart-resource-optimizer.workflow.yaml

Then, in your tenant:

  1. Download the file: in the Explorer, right-click .devcontainer/yaml/gen/smart-resource-optimizer.workflow.yaml → Download.
  2. Open the Workflows app and choose Upload, then select the file.
  3. The workflow opens as Smart K8s Resource Optimizer ({{DT_SESSION_ID}}). Choose Run.

docs.title: Read the result
docs.text:
When the run is green, select the compute_recommendations task and open its Result: recommendations lists, per workload and container, the current and the new CPU and memory request. The task's Log prints one line per container, for example:

cart/cart: cpu 0m -> 2m, memory 100Mi -> 31Mi

The same query runs from your terminal — this is what you apply in the next step:

showRecommendations

This check proves the recommendations for your cluster can be computed — the same numbers the workflow shows:

docs.title: 5. Apply the Recommendations
docs.text:
The workflow computed the requests; now they go into the cluster. In the original workshop this was a pull request on your fork. Here applyRecommendations does the same change in place: it runs the workflow's query for your cluster, and for every opted-in container patches the workload's CPU and memory requests (raising the memory limit where the new request would exceed it). Kubernetes then rolls the pods with the new values.

Look once more at what will change, then apply it:

showRecommendations
applyRecommendations

Each patched workload is annotated with what was applied and when, so the change is traceable:

kubectl get deployments,statefulsets -n otel-demo \
  -o custom-columns='WORKLOAD:.metadata.name,CPU REQUEST:.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu,MEMORY REQUEST:.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.memory,APPLIED AT:.metadata.annotations.resource-optimization\.dynatrace\.com/applied-at'

This check proves the workloads now run with the recommended requests — a CPU request on every container and the applied-at annotation, neither of which the manifests had:

docs.title: 6. Watch the Gap Shrink
docs.text:
The pods now reserve what they use plus headroom. Dynatrace sees the new requests within a minute or two. Run the query from step 3 again, or this one, which shows CPU requests appear where there were none and memory requests move toward usage:

timeseries {
    cpu_requested = sum(dt.kubernetes.container.requests_cpu),
    cpu_used = max(dt.kubernetes.container.cpu_usage),
    mem_requested = sum(dt.kubernetes.container.requests_memory),
    mem_used = max(dt.kubernetes.container.memory_working_set)
  },
  by:{k8s.workload.name},
  filter: endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") AND k8s.namespace.name == "otel-demo",
  from:now()-1h

Switch the result to a line chart: for each workload, requested steps to just above used at the moment you applied the recommendations.

This check proves Dynatrace now reports CPU requests for your workloads — before step 5 they had none:

docs.title: Where to go from here
docs.text:
• Schedule the workflow. Give it a daily trigger and it keeps recommending as the load changes.
  • GitOps. The original workshop let the workflow open a pull request with the patched manifests — in production, that review step is what keeps a human in the loop.
  • Autoscaling. Right-sized requests are what Horizontal Pod Autoscalers and cluster autoscalers scale on: wrong requests make them scale at the wrong time.
